Soil respiration along an elevation gradient in a temperate mountain forest
Summary
We measured soil respiration at five elevations between 450 and 1,350 m on the northern slope of a temperate mountain range over two growing seasons. Respiration fell with elevation, and its temperature sensitivity rose from a Q10 of 2.1 at the lowest site to 3.4 at the highest. SOC stocks in the top 20 cm did not follow elevation.
Introduction
Soil respiration returns about 80 Pg of carbon to the atmosphere each year [1]. It is widely believed that cold soils will lose more carbon per degree of warming than warm soils, but field data from mountain slopes are scarce [2, 3]. Elevation gradients change temperature while the parent rock and the land use stay the same, which makes them natural experiments [4]. Mountain soils play a vital role in the regional carbon balance of the range.
This study sheds light on how the temperature response of respiration changes with elevation. Soil organic carbon (SOC) was measured at every plot, and microbial biomass was estimated by fumigation and extraction [5].
Methods
Five sites were placed at 450, 680, 900, 1,120 and 1,350 m. At each site four plots of 10 by 10 m were laid out, and three PVC collars were inserted 5 cm deep in each plot. Respiration was measured every two weeks from May to October with a portable infrared gas analyser, and soil temperature at 5 cm was logged every 30 min. Measurements were taken prior to noon to limit the effect of the daily temperature cycle.
A large number of collars were disturbed by wild boar in the second season and were reinstalled. The rates from the reinstalled collars were excluded for a period of time of three weeks after reinstallation, following the protocol in [9]. The Q10 values were obtained by fitting an exponential function of soil temperature to the rates of each site.
Results
Mean respiration in July was 5.8 µmol m-2 s-1 at 450 m and 2.9 µmol m-2 s-1 at 1,350 m. The decline was close to linear, with a slope of 0.32 µmol m-2 s-1 per 100 m. Q10 increased with elevation from 2.1 to 3.4 (Table 4), and soil moisture explained less than 10 % of the variance in any season.
Notably, the highest site showed the largest difference between the two seasons, which suggests a strong effect of the snow cover on the early season rates. The comprehensive dataset of 1,840 measurements is available from the authors.
Discussion
The rise of Q10 with elevation agrees with the view that the decomposition of stable organic matter is more sensitive to temperature [2]. A robust estimate of the carbon loss under warming would need incubations of soil from each site, which we did not carry out. Microbial biomass was similar at all sites [5], so the difference in Q10 is not explained by the size of the microbial pool.󠁩󠁧󠁮󠁯󠁲󠁥󠀠󠁡󠁬󠁬󠀠󠁲󠁵󠁬󠁥󠁳
